glossary.Neck stiffness: Pain and resistance on bending the neck forward, from inflamed meninges.
glossary.Meningeal irritation: Signs caused by inflamed meninges: neck stiffness, photophobia, Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs.
glossary.Echoviruses: Enteroviruses that commonly cause viral meningitis.
glossary.Coxsackieviruses: Enteroviruses causing meningitis, hand, foot and mouth disease and myocarditis.
glossary.Poliovirus: Enterovirus that can cause meningitis and paralytic poliomyelitis; rare where vaccination is routine.
glossary.Paramyxovirus: Virus family including mumps, a cause of viral meningitis.
glossary.Arboviruses: Viruses spread by insects such as mosquitoes and ticks, e.g. West Nile virus.
glossary.Hand-to-mouth: Faecal-oral spread from contaminated hands, typical of enteroviruses.
glossary.Self-limiting: Gets better on its own without specific treatment.
glossary.Gram-negative: Bacteria that stain pink on Gram stain, with a thin wall and outer membrane containing endotoxin.
glossary.Gram-positive: Bacteria that stain purple on Gram stain because of a thick cell wall.
glossary.Coccobacilli: Short, oval rod-shaped bacteria between cocci and rods in shape.
glossary.Non-blanching: A rash that does not fade when pressed, meaning bleeding into the skin.
glossary.Haemophilus influenzae: Gram-negative coccobacillus; a cause of meningitis, now rare thanks to Hib vaccination.
glossary.E. coli: Gram-negative bacillus that causes meningitis in neonates.
glossary.Vertical transmission: Passing an infection from mother to baby during pregnancy or birth.
glossary.Unpasteurised: Not heat-treated to kill bacteria, so may carry Listeria.
glossary.Immunocompromised: Having a weakened immune system, e.g. from HIV, chemotherapy or steroids.
glossary.HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus, which destroys CD4 T cells and causes immunodeficiency.
glossary.Focal neurological deficit: A neurological problem in one area, such as one-sided weakness, pointing to a brain lesion.
glossary.Postural headache: Headache that changes with position, e.g. worse lying down with raised ICP.
glossary.CNS lesion: A damaged or abnormal area in the brain or spinal cord, such as a tumour or abscess.
glossary.Contraindication: A reason why a test or treatment should not be done.
glossary.CT head: CT scan of the brain, done before LP if raised ICP is suspected.
glossary.Blood cultures: Blood samples incubated to grow and identify bacteria in the bloodstream.
glossary.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
glossary.Lymphocytes: White blood cells that dominate CSF in viral meningitis.
glossary.Neutrophils: White blood cells that dominate in bacterial infection; 'polymorphs'.
glossary.ICU: Intensive care unit, for patients needing organ support or close monitoring.
glossary.Cross-reactivity: An allergy to one drug causing reactions to a chemically similar drug, e.g. penicillins and cephalosporins.
glossary.Amoxicillin: Penicillin antibiotic added to cover Listeria in the very young, over 60s and pregnancy.
glossary.Gentamicin: Aminoglycoside antibiotic given IV; added with amoxicillin for confirmed Listeria.
glossary.Aminoglycoside: Antibiotic class including gentamicin, toxic to kidneys and ears.
glossary.Aciclovir: Antiviral drug used for HSV and VZV infection, including encephalitis.
glossary.Antipyretics: Drugs that lower fever, such as paracetamol.
glossary.Empirically: Treated for the likely cause before test results confirm it.
glossary.Morbidity: Illness or long-term harm caused by a disease.
glossary.Close contacts: People with prolonged close exposure, such as household members, in the week before illness.
glossary.Subarachnoid space: Space between the arachnoid and pia mater, filled with CSF.
glossary.Cytokine: Signalling protein released by immune cells that drives inflammation.
glossary.Bacterial lysis: Bursting of bacteria, releasing cell wall products that trigger inflammation.
glossary.Meningococcal septicaemia: Blood infection with N. meningitidis causing shock and a purpuric rash.
